title: To counter AI misinformation, invest in skills, literacy
where: The Ideas Page, page 9 (Tim Curtis, UNESCO)
syllabus: GS3 › Internal security: role of media and social networking sites; Cyber security; Science and technology: AI · GS2 › Education (digital and media literacy); Elections · GS4 › Ethics in media and technology; Role of education in inculcating values
summary: UNESCO's South Asia head argues that laws and AI labels cannot keep pace with AI-made misinformation; India must build media and information literacy (MIL) for all, with platforms, newsrooms and creators sharing the job.
ideas: From access to judgement: generative AI makes convincing fakes cheap, so the question is no longer how to find information but how to judge what is reliable. Media and information literacy (MIL) is the answer.
With generative AI making fakes cheap, the challenge has shifted from accessing information to judging it, which makes media and information literacy essential.
Connectivity is not capability: India has over a billion internet subscribers, but few can navigate the information space; platforms reward emotionally charged content, which deepens polarisation.
India's billion internet users show connectivity, not capability: only 18% of adults can file a cybercrime complaint online.
Misinformation does most harm in crises and elections, when people most need reliable information.
Misinformation is most dangerous in crises and elections, as out-of-context flood videos in Nepal and a fake AI audio in Slovakia's election show.

Laws and labels are not enough: labelling AI content helps, but no law or detection tool can match the speed of synthetic content; people need skills, through trained teachers, local-language materials, and outreach beyond classrooms to rural people, women and persons with disabilities.
No law or detection tool can keep pace with AI fakes; lasting defence lies in citizens' skills, taught in local languages and beyond classrooms.

'We All Play a Part': platforms must be transparent about algorithms, label synthetic media and moderate beyond English and Hindi; newsrooms must explain how they verify; creators need verification skills and ethics.
Countering misinformation is a shared duty: transparent platforms, newsrooms that explain verification, and creators trained in ethics.
MIL is an investment in democracy: children grow up in AI-shaped feeds before they can question them, so MIL builds critical thinking, social trust and collective resilience.
Media literacy is not just safe technology use; it is an investment in critical thinking, social trust and democratic resilience.

trend.t: Social media has moved through the papers from a tool of terror (ISIS recruitment 2015, non-state actors 2016) to a security challenge (social media and encryption 2024) to fake news and its regulation (IT Rules 2026). GS4 has added the ethics of social media (2025) and of AI (2024, 2026).
trend.watch: Social media and misinformation have come in four GS3 papers and in GS4 2025, and AI in 2023, 2024 and 2026. AI-driven misinformation joins both threads and is a must-study topic.

title: Everyone's duty in the information age
news: UNESCO's South Asia head says platforms, newsrooms, creators and citizens must all fight AI-made misinformation.
syllabus: Ethical issues in media and technology · Role of education in inculcating values
link: Sharing information carries responsibility: platforms owe transparency, creators owe verification, and citizens owe a pause before forwarding.
question: As a district collector during floods, you find doctored videos spreading panic on social media. How will you respond while respecting freedom of expression?

title: Privacy versus the public's right to know
news: News publishers have challenged the data protection law for requiring a person's consent before journalists process their data.
syllabus: Information sharing and transparency in government · Ethical issues in media
link: Respect for individual privacy must be weighed against the public's right to know about matters of public interest.
question: As an editor, you hold verified evidence of a senior official's misuse of public funds, but he invokes his privacy and refuses consent. What will you do and why?

title: AI, layoffs and an ethical work culture
news: Microsoft offered 'voluntary' exits to 60,000 staff; TCS cut about 12,000 jobs in 2025, mainly middle and senior managers, as AI reshapes work.
syllabus: Work culture · Ethical concerns and dilemmas in private institutions
link: Technological disruption tests whether firms act with honesty, fairness and care for workers' livelihoods and mental health.
question: As HR head of an IT firm adopting AI, you must cut 20% of staff. How will you manage the transition ethically, keeping in mind employees' livelihoods and mental health?
